## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

Introduction to Business is presented as a survey textbook whose object is "the basic structures upon which the business world is built: how it is organized, what outside forces influence it, and where it is heading" [V] (Ch 1, "Introduction"). The book frames business as an applied discipline whose practitioners must integrate perspectives across functional areas — economics, ethics, global trade, ownership forms, entrepreneurship, management, organisational design, HR, motivation, operations, marketing, distribution, technology, accounting, finance, securities markets, careers, and the legal/tax environment — rather than mastering any one in isolation [AR]. The book's organising premise is that the survivor businesses are "those that understand that change is the one constant in the business environment" and "pay attention to the business environment in which they operate and the trends that affect all businesses and then successfully adapt to those trends" [V] (Ch 1, "Introduction").

A second load-bearing claim runs through the volume: that businesses operate in dynamic external environments composed of seven sub-environments (economic, political-and-legal, demographic, social, competitive, global, technological) over which managers have little direct control but to which they must continuously adapt [AR] (Ch 1.2, "Understanding the Business Environment"). The text's strategic-management argument is that "managers are primarily adapters to, rather than agents of, change" [V] (Ch 1.2). The internal environment — supplies, employees, products, locations — is controlled by managers; the external environment is largely beyond their control and changes constantly.

A third load-bearing claim is that *stakeholder consideration* is integral to business success and to corporate social responsibility (CSR). CSR rests on a four-component pyramid — economic responsibility (the foundation), legal responsibility, ethical responsibility, and philanthropic responsibility — and "the stakeholders of a business are its employees, its customers, the general public, and its investors" [V] (Ch 2.4, "Responsibilities to Stakeholders"). Drucker is invoked: "we should look first at what an organization does *to* society and second at what it can do *for* society" [AP, citing Drucker] (Ch 2.3, "Understanding Social Responsibility").

A fourth load-bearing claim is that effective management is a process built around four functions — planning, organising, leading, and controlling — performed across three management levels (top, middle, supervisory) using three skill types (technical, human-relations, conceptual). Leadership style varies along an autocratic-participative-free-rein continuum; situational leadership selects among them based on the maturity and competency of those completing the task [AR] (Ch 6, "Management and Leadership in Today's Organizations"). The 21st-century manager faces crises, technology proliferation, and globalisation as continuing trends.

## Part I: Economic systems and the business environment (Ch 1)

The chapter-opening Exploring Business Careers feature, "Team Rubicon: Disaster Relief and a Sense of Purpose", draws on the organisation's website and press sources [BT, Hrywna; Dickman]. It presents not-for-profits as "an undeniable force in the business world" [V] whose shift away from profit lets them pursue missions of social improvement, and holds that to be effective in one "a person must share the organization’s vision" [V]. Founded by marines Jake Wood and William McNulty after the 2010 Haiti earthquake, Team Rubicon pairs military veterans with first responders for disaster relief and offers veterans a purpose, a sense of community and self-worth; its staff roles mirror those of a for-profit firm, and in 2016 it trained 8,000 veterans and first responders and responded to 46 disasters [BT, Hrywna; Dickman] (Ch 1, "Team Rubicon: Disaster Relief and a Sense of Purpose").

### What is a business

A *business* is "an organization that strives for a profit by providing goods and services desired by its customers" [V] (Ch 1.1, "The Nature of Business"). *Goods* are tangible items manufactured by businesses; *services* are intangible offerings (Ch 1.1). Businesses create the goods and services that determine a country's *standard of living* — "the output of goods and services people can buy with the money they have" [V] (Ch 1.1) — and contribute to *quality of life*, "the general level of human happiness based on such things as life expectancy, educational standards, health, sanitation, and leisure time" [V] (Ch 1.1).

A direct relationship runs between *risk* (potential to lose time and money or fail to accomplish goals) and *profit*: greater risks support greater potential profit (or loss) [AP] (Ch 1.1). The Sony-Apple example anchors this claim: Sony lost ground to Apple in personal music after misjudging the digital music format, while Apple "quickly grabbed the lion's share of the digital music market" [AE] (Ch 1.1). *Not-for-profit organisations* are organisations that exist "to achieve some goal other than the usual business goal of profit" [V] (Ch 1.1, "Not-for-Profit Organizations"); over 1.5 million U.S. nongovernmental not-for-profits contribute "more than $900 billion annually to the U.S. economy" [V] (Ch 1.1).

### Factors of production

Four traditional inputs are common to all productive activity: natural resources, labor (human resources), capital, and entrepreneurship. Entrepreneurs range from Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates and Google founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page to many thousands of founders whose companies stay small yet "make a major contribution to the U.S. economy" [V] [AE] (Ch 1.1, "Factors of Production: The Building Blocks of Business"). Many experts add *knowledge* as a fifth factor [AP] (Ch 1.1, "Factors of Production: The Building Blocks of Business"). The text takes the position that "today's competitive environment places a premium on knowledge and learning over physical resources" [V] (Ch 1.1). The number of U.S. *knowledge workers* has doubled over the last 30 years, with an estimated 2 million knowledge job openings annually (Ch 1.1).

The section's Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "StickerGiant Embraces Change", draws on the company's website and press sources [BT, Burlingham; Strauss; Rusch; Peterson]. It opens on the claim that entrepreneurs "typically are not afraid to take risks or change the way they do business if it means there is a better path to success" [V], and follows John Fischer of Longmont, Colorado, from a 2000 election bumper sticker to an online sticker store, a 2011 shift to custom orders, and in 2012 open-book management: sharing the company's financials with employees at a weekly meeting so they feel part of the operation and are empowered to embrace change or suggest ideas [BT, Burlingham; Strauss; Rusch; Peterson]. Investment in laser-finishing equipment lets the firm make custom stickers in large quantities overnight; it reports $10 million in annual sales and nearly 40 employees [BT, Burlingham; Strauss; Rusch; Peterson] (Ch 1.1, "StickerGiant Embraces Change").

### Seven environmental forces

The business environment decomposes into seven sub-environments [AP] (Ch 1.2, Exhibit 1.4): economic, political and legal, demographic, social, competitive, global, and technological. Managers have control over *internal* operations (supplies, employees, products, locations) but the *external* environmental conditions are "generally beyond the control of management and change constantly" [V] (Ch 1.2). The book's strategic-management argument follows: "managers are primarily adapters to, rather than agents of, change" [V] (Ch 1.2).

Demographic shifts surface across the discussion: U.S. minorities will rise from more than 38% of population to 56% by 2060 (U.S. Census Bureau projection) [V] (Ch 1.2, "Demographic Factors"); millennials surpassed baby boomers as America's largest generation in 2017 (Ch 1.2). Today's workforce spans five generations: Generation Z (recent grads), millennials and Generation X (30s-40s), baby boomers (50s-60s), and traditionalists (70s+) (Ch 1.8, "Changing Workforce Demographics").

The Social Factors discussion carries a Managing Change feature, "Balancing Comes Easy at H&R Block", drawn from company pages and press sources [BT, Hess; Bahler; Ritlop]. H&R Block, with more than 70,000 employees and seasonal workers, headed Indeed's 2017 list of the 20 firms with the best work-life balance, drawn from more than 10 million employee reviews; Indeed's Paul Wolfe names organisational empathy as a key factor, and none of the tech companies known for generous perks made the list [BT, Hess; Bahler; Ritlop]. The point for the section is that supporting work-life balance in a schedule-driven industry helps employees and "also helps H&R Block retain workers in a tight labor market" [V] (Ch 1.2, "Balancing Comes Easy at H&R Block").

The Changing Workforce Demographics discussion carries a Managing Change feature, "EY Makes Diversity and Inclusion a Top Priority", drawn from company pages and press sources [BT, Donnelly]. EY topped DiversityInc's 2017 list of top companies for diversity, and the feature argues that with a diverse workforce becoming the norm, an occasional seminar on diversity is no longer enough [BT, Donnelly]. Global diversity and inclusion officer Karyn Twaronite favours a simple, ongoing approach: the PTR (preference, tradition, and requirement) tool asks managers to examine their preference for candidates like themselves and traditional assumptions about a role, and to select on the job's requirements, so it "gives people a way to question the status quo without accusing colleagues of being biased" [V]. EY also sponsors professional network groups for networking, informal mentoring and leadership skills [BT, Donnelly] (Ch 1.8, "EY Makes Diversity and Inclusion a Top Priority").

### Three economic systems plus mixed

The world's major economic systems fall into broad categories: capitalism (private enterprise), planned economies (communism and socialism), and mixed economies (Ch 1.3, "Global Economic Systems"). *Capitalism* is "based on competition in the marketplace and private ownership of the factors of production (resources)" [V] (Ch 1.3); a capitalist system guarantees "the right to own property, the right to make a profit, the right to make free choices, and the right to compete" [V] (Ch 1.3). *Communism* is the opposite: government owns virtually all resources and controls all markets (Ch 1.3). *Socialism* is an intermediate form: basic industries owned by the government or under strong government control, with smaller businesses privately owned (Ch 1.3). *Mixed economies* (Canada, Sweden, UK) combine elements; the U.S. economy "leans toward pure capitalism, but it uses government policies to promote economic stability and growth" [V] (Ch 1.3, "Mixed Economic Systems").

Table 1.1 compares the four systems row by row [AP] (Ch 1.3, Table 1.1). Ownership: private with minimal government ownership (capitalism); government owns all or most enterprises (communism); government owns basic industries such as railroads and utilities, with very high taxation to redistribute income (socialism); private ownership with government control of some enterprises and a typically large private sector (mixed). Control of markets: complete freedom of trade; complete government control; some markets controlled and some free, with significant central planning and rarely profitable state enterprises run by bureaucrats; some markets, such as nuclear energy and the post office, controlled or highly regulated. Worker incentives: strong because owners retain profits; no incentive to work hard or produce quality products; capitalist incentives in the private sector and planned-economy incentives in the public sector; capitalist incentives in the private sector and limited ones in the public sector. Management: owners or professional managers with little government interference; centralised government bureaucracy with little or no flexibility at factory level; significant government planning, with bureaucrats running government enterprises; private sector like capitalism and public sector like socialism. The 2020 forecast is continued steady growth for capitalism (United States), no growth and perhaps disappearance for communism (Cuba, North Korea), stability with probable slight growth for socialism (Finland, India, Israel), and continued growth for mixed economies (Great Britain, France, Sweden, Canada) [AP] (Ch 1.3, Table 1.1).

### Macroeconomic goals and tools

Three main macroeconomic goals: economic growth, full employment, and price stability (Ch 1.4, "Macroeconomics: The Big Picture"). *Gross domestic product (GDP)* — "the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a nation's borders each year" [V] (Ch 1.4) — is the most basic measure of growth. The U.S. has been growing at 3-4% annually; China at 6-7% (Ch 1.4). *Business cycles* are upward and downward changes in economic activity; a *recession* is "a decline in GDP that lasts for two consecutive quarters" [V] (Ch 1.4). The 2007-2009 recession ended June 2009 (Ch 1.4).

*Full employment* is defined operationally as 94-96% of those available to work having jobs (Ch 1.4, "Keeping People on the Job"). Four types of unemployment are catalogued: frictional (short-term, between-jobs, not cycle-related), structural (mismatch between jobs and skills), cyclical (downturn-driven), and seasonal (Ch 1.4, "Types of Unemployment"). *Inflation* is rising prices; *purchasing power* is "the value of what money can buy" [V] (Ch 1.4, "Keeping Prices Steady"). Two causes of inflation: *demand-pull* (too much money chasing too few goods) and *cost-push* (input costs push prices up); inflation is measured by the consumer price index (CPI, retail prices) and the producer price index (PPI, producer and wholesale prices) (Ch 1.4).

The government uses *monetary policy* and *fiscal policy* to achieve macroeconomic goals (Ch 1.5, "Achieving Macroeconomic Goals"). Monetary policy is "a government's programs for controlling the amount of money circulating in the economy and interest rates" [V] (Ch 1.5); the Federal Reserve System (the Fed) controls the money supply and signals through the federal funds rate. *Contractionary policy* tightens money supply (raises rates); *expansionary policy* loosens it (Ch 1.5). Fiscal policy is "its program of taxation and spending" [V] (Ch 1.5). When government spending exceeds tax revenues, the result is a *federal budget deficit*; the accumulated total is the *national debt* (Ch 1.5).

### Microeconomics: supply and demand

*Demand* is "the quantity of a good or service that people are willing to buy at various prices" [V]; *supply* is the quantity businesses make available at various prices (Ch 1.6, "Microeconomics: Zeroing in on Businesses and Consumers"). The intersection is the *equilibrium* price and quantity. Factors that shift demand: buyers' incomes, preferences, prices of substitutes, expectations about future prices, and number of buyers. Factors that shift supply: technology, resource prices, prices of other products that can be made with the same resources, number of suppliers, and taxes (Ch 1.6, Table 1.2).

### Four market structures

Four types of competitive structure are catalogued (Ch 1.7, "Competing in a Free Market"):

- *Perfect (pure) competition*: many small firms, similar products, good information, easy entry. Approximated by farm products such as wheat and corn [AP].
- *Pure monopoly*: one firm is the industry; high barriers to entry; subject to government regulation. Public utilities, U.S. Postal Service [AE].
- *Monopolistic competition*: many firms with close-but-differentiated substitutes; relatively easy entry; firms have some pricing power through differentiation. Clothing and consumer products [AE].
- *Oligopoly*: a few firms produce most or all output; large capital requirements limit entry. Boeing-Airbus, Apple-Google smartphone OS [AE].

## Part II: Ethics, social responsibility, and stakeholders (Ch 2)

The chapter-opening Exploring Business Careers feature, "Playing with a Purpose at Hasbro", draws on company materials and press sources [BT, Goldner; Gurdus; Burke; Belliveau]. Hasbro, first in Corporate Responsibility magazine's 2017 ranking of the 100 best corporate citizens, is presented as a company that integrates CSR throughout the organisation and focuses it on four areas: product safety (its highest priority, backed by a five-step quality assurance process that also binds third-party factories), environmental sustainability, human rights and ethical sourcing, and community, where it made close to $15 million in financial contributions and product donations in 2016 [BT, Goldner; Gurdus; Burke; Belliveau]. The feature closes on Hasbro as a storytelling business whose CSR efforts "tell the story of an ethical, responsible organization" [V] (Ch 2, "Playing with a Purpose at Hasbro").

### Personal ethical philosophies

*Ethics* is "a set of moral standards for judging whether something is right or wrong" [V] (Ch 2.1, "Understanding Business Ethics"). The text catalogues four philosophical frames for individual ethics:

- *Justice as fairness*: "an equitable distribution of the burdens and rewards that society has to offer" [V] (Ch 2.1).
- *Utilitarianism*: action assessed by "consequences" and "the greatest good for the greatest number" [V] (Ch 2.1). Limitations: nearly impossible to predict effects on many people; involves winners and losers; some "costs" are unacceptable to segments of society regardless of aggregate.
- *Deontology*: people should meet their obligations and duties; the ethical correctness lies in upholding duty itself, not in welfare consequences (Ch 2.1, "Following Our Obligations and Duties").
- *Individual rights*: human rights (life, freedom, pursuit of happiness) and legal rights (constitutional protections) serve as ethical guides and "cannot be arbitrarily taken away" [AP] (Ch 2.1).

### Eleven categories of unethical activity

The Brigham Young University researchers' classification is reproduced (Ch 2.1, "Recognizing Unethical Business Activities"): taking things that don't belong to you; saying things you know are not true; giving or allowing false impressions; buying influence or engaging in a conflict of interest; hiding or divulging information; taking unfair advantage; committing improper personal behavior; abusing power and mistreating individuals; permitting organizational abuse; violating rules; and condoning unethical actions [BT].

### Three organisational tools for ethical conduct

Organisations encourage ethical conduct through (Ch 2.2, "How Organizations Influence Ethical Conduct"):

- *Leading by example*: leaders' patterns of behavior establish what is acceptable. Ben Cohen's policy at Ben & Jerry's of no salary more than seven times the lowest-paid worker is presented as an example [AE] (Ch 2.2, "Leading by Example").
- *Ethics training programs*: 80%+ of U.S. companies provide some form (Ch 2.2). Table 2.1 gives an ethical dilemma used in employee training: middle manager Bill Gannon finds many areas of subpar performance in his employee Robert Talbot's work, including a major client's complaint, while his boss Dana Johnson will not accept negative comments on Robert's evaluation and a previous manager who rated Robert badly is no longer with the company; the discussion questions ask what ethical issues the case raises, what courses of action Bill could take, and whether he should confront Dana or Dana's boss [AE] (Ch 2.2, Table 2.1).
- *Formal codes of ethics*: provide knowledge of what the firm expects; effective only when senior management abides by them and emphasises them regularly (Ch 2.2, "Establishing a Formal Code of Ethics").

Two decision tests are added: the *feelings test* (after deciding, do I sleep well or feel discomfort?) and the *newspaper or social media test* (how would the front page describe my decision?) (Ch 2.2, "Making the Right Decision"). The tests come after three prior questions: does the action break a law, does it violate the company's code of ethics, and does it meet one's own ethical philosophy (Ch 2.2). The feelings test asks "How does it make me feel?" [V]; discomfort after a decision can show up as a loss of sleep or appetite, and "Those feelings of conscience can serve as a future guide in resolving ethical dilemmas" [V]. Of the newspaper test the text says: "This test is helpful in spotting and resolving potential conflicts of interest" [V] (Ch 2.2, "Making the Right Decision").

The section's Customer Satisfaction and Quality feature, "Campbell’s Adds CSR to Its Recipe", draws on company and press sources [BT, Seiffert; Hurst; Stevenson]. Under CEO Denise Morrison (who retired in July 2018), the Campbell Soup Company moved from processed soup towards organics and fresh food, acquiring Bolthouse Farms, Garden Fresh Gourmet and Plum Organics, and was named one of Corporate Responsibility magazine's Best Corporate Citizens in 2017 [BT, Seiffert; Hurst; Stevenson]. Morrison is quoted: "We can make a profit and make a difference" [V]. The feature links the shift to a 20 percent rise in the share price over two years and describes a healthy communities initiative in Camden, New Jersey, funding community gardens, food pantries and nutrition education, since extended to Detroit and Norwalk [BT, Seiffert; Hurst; Stevenson] (Ch 2.2, "Campbell’s Adds CSR to Its Recipe").

### The pyramid of corporate social responsibility

*Corporate social responsibility (CSR)* is "the concern of businesses for the welfare of society as a whole" [V]; it "consists of obligations beyond those required by law or union contract" [V] (Ch 2.3, "Managing a Socially Responsible Business"). The pyramid has four components stacked from foundation upward (Ch 2.3, Exhibit 2.4): economic responsibility (the foundation — without profit, the others don't matter), legal responsibility (obey the law), ethical responsibility (do what is right, just, and fair), and philanthropic responsibility (be a good corporate citizen). Business activity sorts into three categories: illegal-and-irresponsible; irresponsible-but-legal; and legal-and-responsible (the vast majority) [AP] (Ch 2.3).

Between the irresponsible-but-legal and legal-and-responsible categories sits a Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "Badger Company Founder Walks the Walk", drawn from company and press sources [BT, Feldman]. Carpenter Bill Whyte mixed olive oil and beeswax into a balm for his cracked hands and built W.S. Badger Company, which uses organic and natural ingredients and is run with family members on ethical and social principles [BT, Feldman]. Certification as a B Corp, which requires rigorous standards for transparency, accountability, and social and environmental performance, "has helped the company organize how it operates" [V]: top full-time pay is capped at five times the lowest, now $15 an hour; profits are shared with employees and all join a bonus plan; new parents may bring babies to work; and 10 percent of pre-tax profits goes each year to nonprofits for children's health and welfare [BT, Feldman] (Ch 2.3, "Badger Company Founder Walks the Walk").

### Stakeholders defined

*Stakeholders* are "the individuals or groups to whom a business has a responsibility": employees, customers, the general public, and investors [V] (Ch 2.4, "Responsibilities to Stakeholders"). The book systematically iterates through each stakeholder group:

- *Employees*: provide jobs; safe and discrimination-free working environment; empowerment to make decisions (Ch 2.4, "Responsibility to Employees").
- *Customers*: deliver what's promised; honesty and forthrightness (Ch 2.4, "Responsibility to Customers").
- *Society*: jobs, goods, services, taxes; certified Benefit Corporations (B Corps) reach a higher standard (Ch 2.4, "Responsibility to Society"). Environmental protection, corporate philanthropy (more than $19 billion annually in U.S. corporate philanthropy) [V] (Ch 2.4, "Corporate Philanthropy").
- *Investors*: economic responsibility; *social investing* is investing limited to securities matching ethical/social beliefs; assets invested using socially responsible strategies total >$7 trillion [V] (Ch 2.4, "Responsibilities to Investors").

The Responsibility to Society discussion carries an Ethics in Practice feature, "This Fish Story Has a Tasting Ending", drawn from company and press sources [BT, Santen; Crawford; Buchanan; Harrison]. Former sea captain and organic-cotton entrepreneur Duncan Berry, working on an Oregon initiative to preserve marine habitats, found the commercial fishing industry in disrepair and concluded that consumers were the group missing from efforts to improve it; he co-founded Fishpeople Seafood in 2012 after realising that most fish is eaten in restaurants because people think preparing it at home is too hard [BT, Santen; Crawford; Buchanan; Harrison]. The company's mission rests on transparency about where its seafood comes from and how it is processed and handled: a code on every package traces the seafood "down to the fisherman who caught it" [V], and its Toledo, Oregon, plant pays a livable wage with health insurance [BT, Santen; Crawford; Buchanan; Harrison] (Ch 2.4, "This Fish Story Has a Tasting Ending").

### Trends: strategic giving and the new social contract

*Strategic giving* ties philanthropy to a company's mission/goals and targets donations to communities where the company does business (Ch 2.5, "Changes in Corporate Philanthropy"). The *social contract between employer and employee* has four aspects: compensation, management, culture, and learning and development (Ch 2.5, "A Social Contract between Employer and Employee").

## Part III: Global marketplace (Ch 3)

The chapter-opening Exploring Business Careers feature, "Mike Schlater, Domino's Pizza", draws on company and press sources [BT, Wilhelm]. It follows Schlater from pizza delivery driver to holder of the first international Domino's franchise, in Winnipeg in 1983, and on to president of Domino's of Canada, which operates more than 440 stores [BT, Wilhelm]. Entering Canada meant finding international suppliers and getting them approved, which the box presents as a general challenge of new global markets: “companies must undertake an extensive review of potential new suppliers to ensure consistent product quality” [V]. Its point for the chapter is the value of master franchisees, who control all operations within a country under a licensing agreement and bring local knowledge of political, cultural and economic differences, for example that “in Japanese, there is no word for pepperoni” [V] (Ch 3, "Mike Schlater, Domino's Pizza").

### Why nations trade

The principles of *absolute advantage* (a country produces something cheaper or has it exclusively) and *comparative advantage* (each country specialises in what it produces "most readily and cheaply" and trades for goods foreign countries produce most readily and cheaply) anchor the case for trade [V] (Ch 3.2, "Why Nations Trade"). *Free trade* permits people and businesses to buy and sell where they please without restrictions; *protectionism* protects home industries through artificial barriers (tariffs, quotas) (Ch 3.2).

### Trade barriers

*Natural barriers*: distance and language (Ch 3.3, "Barriers to Trade"). *Tariff barriers*: a *tariff* is "a tax imposed by a nation on imported goods" [V] (Ch 3.3); *protective tariffs* make imported products less attractive to buyers than domestic. *Nontariff barriers*: import quotas, embargoes (complete bans), buy-national regulations, exchange controls (laws requiring foreign-exchange earnings to be sold to a control agency, usually the central bank) (Ch 3.3).

### Fostering global trade

*Antidumping laws* address *dumping* — "the practice of charging a lower price for a product (perhaps below cost) in foreign markets than in the firm's home market" [V] (Ch 3.4, "Antidumping Laws"). The *World Trade Organization* replaced the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT, created 1948); the WTO has emerged as "the world's most powerful institution for reducing trade barriers and opening markets" [V] (Ch 3.4, "Trade Negotiations and the World Trade Organization"). Two international financial organisations support trade: the *World Bank* (low-interest loans to developing nations) and the *International Monetary Fund (IMF)* (short-term loans to nations unable to meet budgetary expenses; lender of last resort) (Ch 3.4, "The World Bank and International Monetary Fund").

### Economic communities and trade agreements

The *North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)* (ratified 1993) created the world's largest free-trade zone (US, Canada, Mexico) (Ch 3.5, "North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA)"). *Mercosur* includes Peru, Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay (Ch 3.5). *CAFTA* (Central America Free Trade Agreement, 2005) includes Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua plus the US (Ch 3.5). The *European Union* (EU) increased integration of 28 European nations (as of 2018; Brexit pending) through common institutions, common currency (euro), and EU-level decision-making (Ch 3.5, "The European Union"). Exhibit 3.6 maps the 28 member states and five candidate countries (Albania, the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, Turkey) [AP] (Ch 3.5, Exhibit 3.6).

### Six entry modes for the global marketplace

Companies enter global trade through six modes ordered roughly by risk and commitment (Ch 3.6, "Participating in the Global Marketplace"):

1. *Exporting*: selling domestically produced products to foreign buyers (least complicated, least risky).
2. *Licensing*: licensor agrees to let licensee use a manufacturing process, trademark, patent, trade secret, or other proprietary knowledge in exchange for royalties.
3. *Franchising*: a form of licensing.
4. *Contract manufacturing*: a foreign firm manufactures private-label goods under a domestic firm's brand.
5. *Joint ventures*: domestic firm buys part of a foreign company or joins with one to create a new entity.
6. *Direct foreign investment*: active ownership of a foreign company or overseas manufacturing/marketing facilities — greatest reward and risk.

*Countertrade* is when "part or all of the payment for goods or services is in the form of other goods or services" [V] (Ch 3.6, "Countertrade"); the U.S. Commerce Department says ~30% of all international trade involves countertrade.

The section's Managing Change feature, "Managing the Drop in Oil Prices", draws on press sources [BT, Reed and Krauss; Biers; Tejani]. It describes crude oil's fall from $90 a barrel in 2014 to $45–$60 in early 2015 and how oil company managers responded: Chevron trimmed planned capital spending by $5 billion, cutting 1,500 jobs, and Royal Dutch Shell planned to cut 6,500 jobs, while Encana, helped by a low debt-to-equity ratio and above-average growth, planned to raise spending [BT, Reed and Krauss; Biers]. It argues that “reactive short-term strategies can often hurt long-term growth” [V] and sets out alternatives: mergers, performance-improvement programmes, a reviewed and wider supplier base with a lean manufacturing mindset, and new technology, which tends to need higher-skilled workers [BT, Tejani]. It concludes that the “companies that employ multiple strategies to improve efficiency are the ones that will survive and prosper” [V] (Ch 3.6, "Managing the Drop in Oil Prices").

### Threats and opportunities in foreign markets

*Political*: nationalism can lead to expropriation (taking ownership and compensating) or confiscation (without compensation) (Ch 3.7, "Political Considerations"). *Cultural*: language, customs, traditions; the text treats the Mitsubishi Pajero name (Spanish slang) and Coca-Cola Chinese characters (mistranslation) as cautionary examples (Ch 3.7, "Cultural Differences").

Table 3.1 sets out cultural dos and don'ts [AP] (Ch 3.7, Table 3.1). Do: present a business card with both hands in Asian countries and examine one received with care; use a soft-sell approach in Japan; understand the role of religion, since business slows during Ramadan in Muslim countries; and have a local person interpret advertising, since American Airlines' “Fly in Leather” campaign, translated literally, meant “Fly Naked” in Spanish [AE]. Don't: glad-hand, back-slap or use first names at a first business meeting in Asia; fill a French businessperson's wine glass to the top; or open a first meeting in Asia by talking business (Ch 3.7, Table 3.1).

Table 3.2, "Where the Money Is", ranks countries by gross national income (GNI) per capita in US dollars from IMF World Economic Outlook data (April 2017): the top 20 run from Luxembourg (103,199) down to Japan (38,912), with the United States seventh (57,436), and the bottom five run from Madagascar (391) to South Sudan (233) [AP]. Its note defines GNI as a country's gross domestic product plus income received from other countries (such as interest and dividends), less similar payments made to other countries, and defines final goods as goods ultimately consumed rather than used to produce another good: tyres sold to a carmaker are intermediate goods, while the same tyres sold to a consumer are final goods [AP] (Ch 3.7, Table 3.2).

### The impact of multinational corporations

*Multinational corporations* are corporations “that move resources, goods, services, and skills across national boundaries without regard to the country in which their headquarters are located” [V] (Ch 3.8, "The Impact of Multinational Corporations"). Some are so rich and employ so many people that they resemble small countries: the sales of both Exxon and Walmart exceed the GDP of all but a few nations [AE]. The successful ones take political and cultural differences into account, and many global brands (Coca-Cola, Marlboro, Pepsi, Kellogg, Pampers, Nescafe, Gillette) sell much more outside the United States than at home [AP]. The Fortune 500 made over $1.5 trillion in profit in 2016; a weaker dollar helps in slow-growing developed economies such as Europe and Japan, while emerging markets in Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe grow steadily, so that General Electric expects 60 percent of its revenue growth to come from emerging markets over the next decade and Brown-Forman gets a fifth of the sales growth of Jack Daniels from developing markets such as Mexico and Poland [AE] (Ch 3.8, "The Impact of Multinational Corporations").

Table 3.3 lists the world's 11 largest multinational corporations by revenue, adapted from Fortune: Walmart ($482,130 million, United States) leads, followed by three Chinese firms (State Grid, China National Petroleum, Sinopec Group), then Royal Dutch Shell (Netherlands), Exxon Mobil (United States), Volkswagen (Germany), Toyota Motor (Japan), Apple (United States), BP (United Kingdom) and Berkshire Hathaway ($210,821 million, United States) [AP] (Ch 3.8, Table 3.3).

The section's Expanding Around the Globe feature, "U.S. Brands Face Global Competition", draws on press and research sources [BT, Interbrand; Davvetas and Diamantopoulos; Vence]. It argues that “American brands’ domination in the global marketplace is eroding” [V], as European and Asian companies such as Samsung, Toyota, Mercedes Benz and SAP sell top-quality goods as such rather than competing on price. Earl L. Taylor of the Marketing Science Institute is quoted that “Consumers prefer brands that they take to be of higher quality” [V] whatever their country of origin. Four of the five brands at the top of Interbrand's list are still American, but George T. Haley places the largest losses in the middle tier of recognisable brands [BT, Interbrand; Vence]. Pressure comes from Chinese firms (Haier, which bought GE's appliance division in 2016; Kelon; Li Ning), South Korean brands (Samsung, LG, Hyundai) and European brands that are becoming stronger and more consistent [BT] (Ch 3.8, "U.S. Brands Face Global Competition").

### Trends in global competition

Among the trends propelling world trade, the section notes that “technical and managerial skills in both China and India are becoming more important than cheap assembly labor” [V]: China will stay dominant in mass manufacturing, while India is a rising power in software, design, services and precision industry [AP] (Ch 3.9, "The Emergence of China and India").

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "The United Nations Sustainability Development Goals", draws on press, UN and company sources [BT, Kreiner; Embree]. It contrasts corporate social responsibility programmes, whose benefits to profitability are “mostly peripheral” [V], so that short-term pressures such as a drop in demand pull attention back to the bottom line, with the 17 goals UN member nations adopted in 2015 to end poverty, ensure sustainability and ensure prosperity for all within 15 years [BT, Kreiner]. The box lists all 17 goals, from ending poverty and hunger through climate action and ocean conservation to revitalising the global partnership. Albertson's tied goal 14 to World Oceans Day, pledging as one of the largest U.S. seafood retailers that “the wellbeing of people and the sustainability of our oceans are interdependent” [V], and was the first retailer to sell tuna with the fair trade seal; Siemens grounded its support in its company values and defined sustainable development as the means to profitable, long-term growth [BT, Embree] (Ch 3.9, "The United Nations Sustainability Development Goals").

## Part IV: Forms of business ownership (Ch 4)

The chapter-opening Exploring Business Careers feature, "Jessica MacLean, Sole Proprietor", follows a lawyer focused mainly on women's rights through several forms of business organisation [AE]. After clerking in Chicago's sexual harassment office and working for the Cook County state's attorney's office, she moved to corporate law out of burnout, then left it to start her own practice as a sole proprietor, because “I can easily dissolve the business if I find it is not proceeding how I’d planned” [V]; in 2014 she joined a limited liability partnership firm in Chicago [AE]. The box presents sole proprietorships as suited to people who want to work alone, prefer direct control and want the flexibility to sell or close at any time [AP], and closes that “As her needs changed, the form and type of business organization she has worked for has changed also” [V] (Ch 4, "Jessica MacLean, Sole Proprietor").

### Sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation

Three primary forms account for U.S. business: sole proprietorships (72% of businesses, 4% of revenue, 15% of profit), partnerships (10% of businesses, 15% of revenue, 27% of profit), and corporations (18% of businesses, 81% of revenue, 58% of profit) [V] (Ch 4, Table 4.1, U.S. Census, *Statistical Abstract*). The trade-offs:

- *Sole proprietorship*: easy/inexpensive to form; profits go to owner; direct control; freedom from regulation; pass-through taxation; ease of dissolution. Disadvantages: unlimited liability; difficulty raising capital; limited managerial expertise; trouble finding qualified employees; personal time commitment; unstable life; losses are owner's responsibility (Ch 4.1).
- *Partnership*: similar advantages plus availability of capital and diversity of skills; pass-through taxation. Disadvantages: unlimited liability for general partners (limited liability available through limited partnerships and LLPs); potential for conflicts; complexity of profit sharing; difficulty exiting (Ch 4.2). The text includes a discussion of how to choose a partner.
- *Corporation*: limited liability; ease of transferring ownership; unlimited life; ability to attract financing; tax deductions for operating expenses. Disadvantages: double taxation of profits; cost and complexity of formation; more government restrictions (Ch 4.3).

Three corporate variants: *C corporation* (conventional); *S corporation* (hybrid; up to 100 shareholders; one class of stock; pass-through taxation while preserving liability protection); *limited liability company (LLC)* (hybrid; first authorised Wyoming 1977; popular since 1988 IRS ruling; treated like partnership for tax purposes; flexible) (Ch 4.3, "Types of Corporations").

The section's Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "Work-Life Balance Important in Small Business", draws on survey and press sources [BT, Sutter; Di Gangi; Wuu; Galoozis]. Surveys find small business owners work long hours (a Gallup survey finds 39 percent working over 60 hours a week) and 62 percent found the stress of ownership worse than they had imagined, yet over two-thirds were satisfied with their work-life balance and almost 90 percent with being an owner [BT, Sutter; Di Gangi; Wuu]. Gallup's Dennis Jacobe is quoted: “Working hard and long is a natural aspect of the kind of people willing to start their own business” [V]. The box then turns to employees: a study of more than 50,000 U.S. workers found those with a positive work-life balance 11 percent more likely to praise their leaders' ability to set a clear direction, and SHRM research links work-life balance to how employees see their leaders [BT, Galoozis] (Ch 4.1, "Work-Life Balance Important in Small Business").

The section's Managing Change feature, "Pacific Sun’s Golden Glow", draws on press and company sources [BT, Driscoll; Ehlers; Masunaga; Church]. It traces PacSun from a Newport Beach surf shop founded in 1980, whose idea was to be the first surf shop in California's malls, through a 1993 public stock sale as a 60-store company to more than 1,000 stores and 12,000 employees [BT, Driscoll; Ehlers]. The CEO credits listening to young customers, “We listen and we change” [V], backed by weekly vendor open houses and “active brand management” [V]. Facing changing trends and online shopping, PacSun filed for bankruptcy in April 2016 and emerged in September 2016 after cutting debt and closing stores, with its stock turned over to its senior lender, Golden Gate Capital [BT, Masunaga; Church]. The box uses the case to show a firm moving from sole proprietorship to corporate retailing giant [AR] (Ch 4.3, "Pacific Sun’s Golden Glow").

### Cooperatives, joint ventures, franchising

A *cooperative* is "a legal entity with several corporate features, such as limited liability, an unlimited life span, an elected board of directors, and an administrative staff" [V] (Ch 4.4, "Cooperatives"); members pay annual fees and share profits in proportion to contributions. Two types: *buyer cooperatives* (combine purchasing power; Ace Hardware) and *seller cooperatives* (popular in agriculture; Sunkist, Land O'Lakes, Calavo, Ocean Spray, Blue Diamond, CHS Inc.). Cooperative principles per the International Co-operative Alliance: open membership, democratic member control, members' economic participation, autonomy, education and training (Ch 4.4).

A *joint venture* is when "two or more companies form an alliance to pursue a specific project, usually for a specified time period" (Ch 4.4, "Joint Ventures").

*Franchising* is a form of business organisation involving a *franchisor* (supplying the product/service concept) and a *franchisee* (selling the goods or services in a certain geographic area). Franchised businesses provided ~8.9 million direct jobs and $890 billion economic output for the U.S. economy [V] (Ch 4.5, "Franchising: A Popular Trend"). The franchise agreement governs use of name/trademark/logo, operating rules, and financial terms.

The section's Expanding Around the Globe feature, "Setting Up (Sandwich) Shop in China", draws on press and company sources [BT, Adler; Bennett]. It follows Jim Bryant, who became Subway's representative in China after founder Fred DeLuca's 1994 visit, recruiting and training local franchisees in return for half the initial $10,000 franchise fee and one-third of their 8 percent royalty fees [BT, Adler; Bennett]. Because foreign businesses in China had to be joint ventures with local partners, he relied on local relationships for his first store and was swindled out of $200,000; locals did not know how to order or want sandwiches, and in ten years he opened 19 stores, half the number planned [BT, Adler; Bennett]. A Beijing franchisee argues that “Subway should have at least one item tailored to Chinese tastes to show they respect local culture” [V], though tuna salad became the top seller and China now has nearly 600 Subway stores (Ch 4.5, "Setting Up (Sandwich) Shop in China").

### Mergers and acquisitions

Mergers consolidate firms by combining or acquiring; the text frames them as another route to growth and another transaction class subject to antitrust review (Ch 4.6, "Mergers and Acquisitions").

## Part V: Entrepreneurship and small business (Ch 5)

The chapter's opening Exploring Business Careers feature, "Natalie Tessler, Spa Space", draws on company websites and a magazine review [BT, Armstrong]. Tessler left work as a tax attorney at a large Chicago firm because it left her unfulfilled: she wanted neither to practise law nor to work for someone else, and said “I wanted to wake up and be excited for my day” [V]. Drawing on a flair for hospitality, she founded Spa Space, which pairs indulgence with medically sound skin care through a medical advisory board; it opened in 2001 and came through 9/11 and the Great Recession as she refined its target market and services [BT, Armstrong]. The chapter presents her as typical of entrepreneurs who have a vision and pursue it single-mindedly [AP] (Ch 5, "Natalie Tessler, Spa Space").

### Three types of entrepreneurs

*Entrepreneurs* are "people with vision, drive, and creativity, who are willing to take the risk of starting and managing a business to make a profit" [V] (Ch 5.1, "Entrepreneurship Today"). Three types:

- *Classic entrepreneurs*: risk-takers based on innovative ideas; *micropreneurs* start small and stay small (e.g., Miho Inagi's Maruichi Bagel in Tokyo); *growth-oriented entrepreneurs* aim for major-corporation scale (e.g., Jeff Bezos / Amazon).
- *Multipreneurs*: serial entrepreneurs who start a series of companies (Ch 5.1, "Multipreneurs").
- *Intrapreneurs*: apply entrepreneurial creativity within a large corporation; financial backing and salary from employer; less personal risk (Ch 5.1, "Intrapreneurs"). The term was coined by Gifford Pinchot.

The section's Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "Young Entrepreneur Living the Dream", draws on press sources [BT, Gasca; Martin]. Jack Bonneau, told he could have a $400 LEGO Star Wars Death Star only if he paid for it himself, moved from a lemonade stand to one at a local farmers market, where, he says, “There were lots of people who wanted to buy great lemonade from an eight-year-old” [V]. Loans of $5,000 from Young Americas Bank, a Denver bank that lends to children, and then $12,000 funded more stands, mall locations and shop space for other young sellers as Jack’s Stands and Marketplace, which brought in more than $100,000 last year [BT, Gasca; Martin]. The box holds him up, at 11, as having mastered financial literacy, customer service, marketing and sales and other sound business practices [BT, Gasca; Martin] (Ch 5.1, "Young Entrepreneur Living the Dream").

### Nine entrepreneurial traits

Entrepreneurs share a personality profile (Ch 5.2, "The Entrepreneurial Personality"): ambitious, independent, self-confident, risk-takers (preferring moderate risk over high), visionary, creative, energetic, passionate, committed [AP].

The section's Customer Satisfaction and Quality feature, "Ethical Choices Transform Family Business into International Brand", draws on press sources [BT, Bortin; Collins; Katz; Antoine]. When her parents died in a 2002 helicopter crash, 18-year-old Apollonia Poilâne took over the family's Paris bakery; as her Harvard admissions essay put it, “The work of several generations is at stake” [V]. She ran it from Cambridge, Massachusetts while a student, checking bread quality nightly with her Paris production manager, and kept control of decisions, strategy and goals as the “commander of the ship” [V]. The box credits her work ethic and passion for this drive; Poilâne is now an $18 million business with 160 employees that ships more than 200,000 loaves a year to clients in 20 countries [BT, Bortin; Collins; Katz; Antoine] (Ch 5.2, "Ethical Choices Transform Family Business into International Brand").

### Small business in the U.S. economy

*Small businesses* employ about half the U.S. private-sector workforce and represent about half of U.S. economic output (Ch 5.3, "Small Business: Driving America's Growth"). Based on 2014 firm-size data: 80% of the ~29.7 million U.S. businesses have no employees; 89% of those with employees have <20 employees; only ~19,000 have >500 employees (Ch 5, Table 5.1, "Firm Size Data: 2014").

Established small businesses are defined as businesses over five years old employing at least one but fewer than 50 employees. Of these, Table 5.5 (Kauffman Foundation calculations from Business Dynamics Statistics, November 2016) shows 53.07% with 1–4 employees, 23.23% with 5–9, 14.36% with 10–19 and 9.33% with 20–49 [AP] (Ch 5.3, Table 5.5, "Number of Employees, by Percentage of Established Small Businesses").

### Seven steps to starting a business

The Small Business Administration (SBA) checklist (Ch 5.4, "Ready, Set, Start Your Own Business"):

1. Identify your reasons.
2. Self-analysis.
3. Personal skills and experience.
4. Finding a niche.
5. Conduct market research.
6. Plan your start-up: write a business plan.
7. Finances: how to fund your business.

The *business plan* is a written document including general description, owner qualifications, products/services description, market analysis (demand, customers, competition), sales/distribution channels, and financial plan. Two financing modes: *debt* (borrowed funds repaid with interest) and *equity* (funds raised through stock sale) (Ch 5.4, "Financing the Business"). *Angel investors* are individuals or groups providing seed capital; *venture capital* comes from firms specialising in financing small high-growth companies — venture capitalists "buy stock at a very low price" and earn profits by selling at a much higher price when the company goes public (Ch 5.4, "Angel Investors").

Table 5.8 sets out the key elements of a business plan [AP] (Ch 5.4, Table 5.8, "Key Elements of a Business Plan"): an *executive summary*, written after the other sections, that highlights the significant points; a *vision and mission statement* (strategy and business philosophy, optionally company values); a *company overview* (type of company, background, legal form, name and location, objectives, status and history); a *product and/or service plan* (features and benefits that give a competitive advantage, legal protection); a *marketing plan* (target market and customer profile, competition and competitive edge, strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, value proposition, selling approach and distribution channels, promotion and budget, pricing and credit policies); a *management plan* (key players and their qualifications, outside investors or directors, recruiting and training plans); an *operating plan* (operating methods, facilities, quality control, inventory and supply); a *financial plan* (financing needs and sources, historical and 3–5-year pro forma statements, assumptions, breakeven analysis); and an *appendix of supporting documents* (team biographies, values, culture, competitive analysis, testimonials, research summaries).

### Business failure

Business closure causes are interrelated: economic factors, financial causes (inadequate capital, low cash, high expenses), lack of experience, personal reasons (Ch 5.4, "Risky Business"). Inadequate early planning often underlies later problems.

Managing a small business, whether started from scratch or bought, means keeping it going: the owner must be ready to solve problems as they arise and move quickly if market conditions change [AP] (Ch 5.5, "Managing a Small Business").

The Ch 5.5 Managing Change feature, "Learning How to Pivot", draws on press sources [BT, Aspan; Manjoo]. MailChimp's founders, Ben Chestnut and Dan Kurzius, ran a web design firm, Rocket Science Group, and shifted its sales focus from tech companies to airline and travel firms to real estate as the tech bubble burst and 9/11 hit; disliking sales and big-company bureaucracy, they found that small businesses kept asking for email marketing [BT, Aspan; Manjoo]. Not until almost 2009 did they settle on freemium, in Chestnut's words “Let’s just make the whole thing free” [V], charging only above 2,000 recipients and for premium features; users grew from a few hundred thousand to 1 million in a year. The box's lesson is knowing when to change: when an opportunity appears, pivot, especially towards a market one is passionate about [BT, Aspan; Manjoo] (Ch 5.5, "Learning How to Pivot").

## Part VI: Management and leadership (Ch 6)

The chapter's opening Exploring Business Careers feature, "Jalem Getz, BuyCostumes.com/Wantable, Inc.", draws on company and press sources [BT, Engel]. It answers how one comes to work in online costume retail, for Getz, with a passion for dress-up, an eye for business potential and the drive to use a competitive advantage [BT, Engel]. He founded BuyCostumes.com because seasonal mall stores had to be found, staffed, trained and stocked anew each year, whereas the internet gave year-round space with inventory and staff in one warehouse [BT, Engel]. His management maxim is “Inspect what you expect.” [V]: he checks in with employees periodically rather than watching over them, which the box reads as a strong participative leadership style; he later launched the online personal shopping service Wantable in 2012 [BT, Engel] (Ch 6, "Jalem Getz, BuyCostumes.com/Wantable, Inc.").

### Four management functions

*Management* is "the process of guiding the development, maintenance, and allocation of resources to attain organizational goals" [V] (Ch 6.1, "The Role of Management"). The process is built around four functions: planning, organising, leading, and controlling — "a tightly integrated cycle of thoughts and actions" [V] (Ch 6.1). The cycle: anticipate problems/opportunities, design plans → coordinate and allocate resources → guide personnel through implementation → review results, make changes → cycle again. *Efficiency* is "using the least possible amount of resources to get work done"; *effectiveness* is "the ability to produce a desired result" [V] (Ch 6.1).

Table 6.1 sets out what each function involves [AP] (Ch 6.1, Table 6.1, "What Managers Do and Why"): *planning* (set objectives and state mission, examine alternatives, determine needed resources, create strategies to reach objectives); *organising* (design jobs and specify tasks, create organisational structure, staff positions, coordinate work activities, set policies and procedures, allocate resources); *leading* (lead and motivate employees to accomplish organisational goals, communicate with employees, resolve conflicts, manage change); and *controlling* (measure performance, compare it to standards, take action to improve it). The four lead to organisational efficiency and effectiveness, which lead in turn to achievement of the organisation's mission and objectives.

### Four types of planning

Four planning types are distinguished (Ch 6.2, "Planning", Table 6.2):

- *Strategic*: 1-5 years; top management; external environment and entire organisation; broad/general; high uncertainty.
- *Tactical*: less than 1 year; middle management; strategic business units; more specific; moderate certainty.
- *Operational*: current; supervisory management; geographic/functional divisions; specific/concrete; reasonable certainty.
- *Contingency*: identifies alternative courses of action for very unusual or crisis situations. Table 6.2 gives its time frame as when an event occurs or a situation demands; top and middle management; external environment and entire organisation; purpose to meet unforeseen challenges and opportunities; both broad and detailed; reasonable certainty once the event or situation occurs [AP] (Ch 6.2, Table 6.2).

The *mission statement* "states the purpose of the organization and its reason for existing" [V] (Ch 6.2). Table 6.3 illustrates with Twitter's mission (to give everyone the power to create and share ideas and information instantly, without barriers), values (belief in free expression) and strategy (to reach the largest daily audience in the world and be a top revenue-generating Internet company), and names three parts of a company mission statement: purpose, value and action [AP] (Ch 6.2, Table 6.3, "Twitter’s Mission, Values, and Strategy"). Marriott Hotels' Hurricane Maria response is presented as exemplary contingency planning [AE] (Ch 6.2).

The section's Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "Changing Strategy Can Change Your Opportunities", draws on a press source [BT, Bells]. Gordon Bernard, a Milford, Ohio printer that since 1949 had printed only fundraising calendars, bought a $650,000 Xerox iGEN3 digital colour press to bring outsourced work in-house; the press “did more for the company than simply reduce costs” [V], since its cheap short runs and per-piece customisation led management to rethink strategy [BT, Bells]. President Bob Sherman set up a new division, and the firm came to see itself as a marketing services company with printing capabilities, seeking commercial work to fill the off-peak capacity of a seasonal calendar business that made up 97 percent of revenue; managers aimed for the division to bring in 10 percent of revenue within a couple of years [BT, Bells] (Ch 6.2, "Changing Strategy Can Change Your Opportunities").

The section's Managing Change feature, "Boeing Takes Off in New Direction", draws on press sources [BT, Rich; Ostrower; Taylor; Matlack; Holmes]. After decades of competing with Airbus on ever larger planes, Boeing conceded the super-jumbo segment, killed its planned 525-seat 747X, and turned first to planes flying fewer people at higher speeds and then, as jet fuel prices rose, to fuel efficiency: “In the end, Boeing’s strategy changed from plane capacity to jet efficiency.” [V]. The new strategy needed new plans: managers targeted gaps in Airbus's line with the fuel-efficient 787 “Dreamliner,” whose stronger-than-expected orders forced Boeing to change its production plans and speed output, while Airbus's focus on its super-jumbo left its rival A350 behind [BT, Rich; Ostrower; Taylor; Matlack; Holmes] (Ch 6.2, "Boeing Takes Off in New Direction").

### Three managerial levels and three skill types

The managerial pyramid has three levels: top management (CEO, president, vice president); middle management (division heads, departmental managers, regional sales managers); supervisory (first-line) management (Ch 6.3, "Organizing"). Three skills are needed in different proportions: *technical* (most important at supervisory level); *human relations* (important at all levels); *conceptual* (most important at top management) (Ch 6.7, Exhibit 6.8). Promotion increases conceptual demand and decreases technical demand.

### Leadership styles continuum

*Leadership* is "the process of guiding and motivating others toward the achievement of organizational goals" [V] (Ch 6.4, "Leading, Guiding, and Motivating Others"). *Power* is "the ability to influence others to behave in a particular way" [V]. Five primary sources of power are catalogued: *legitimate*, *reward*, *coercive*, *expert*, *referent* (Ch 6.4). The text notes A. G. Lafley at P&G as an example of a leader using all five.

Leadership styles span a continuum (Ch 6.4, "Leadership Styles", Table 6.4):

- *Autocratic*: directive; manager makes most decisions; one-way information flow; military and some production-line settings. The text notes "the trend in organizations today is away from the directive, controlling style of the autocratic leader" [V].
- *Participative*: shares decision-making with group members; encourages discussion. Three sub-types: *democratic* (group votes); *consensual* (all parties must agree); *consultative* (manager confers but retains final authority).
- *Free-rein (laissez-faire)*: manager turns over authority and control to subordinates; assigns tasks; gets involved only if asked. Table 6.4 says the approach works well with highly motivated, experienced, educated personnel. Drawback: if accompanied by unclear expectations and lack of feedback, frustrating for employees.

*Situational leadership* selects among styles based on the maturity and competency levels of those completing the tasks (Ch 6.4). Newly hired employees may respond well to authoritative leadership until they understand the job requirements and can handle routine decisions; once established, they may perform better under a participative or free-rein style (Ch 6.4, "Leadership Styles"). *Empowerment* is "giving employees increased autonomy and discretion to make their own decisions, as well as control over the resources needed to implement those decisions" [V] (Ch 6.4, "Employee Empowerment"). The Norfolk Southern engineer Jeff McCracken's post-Hurricane-Katrina five-mile track rescue is presented as an example of empowered decision-making at a distance from headquarters [AE] (Ch 6.4).

*Corporate culture* is "the set of attitudes, values, and standards of behavior that distinguishes one organization from another" [V] (Ch 6.4, "Corporate Culture"). Culture evolves over time and is influenced by founders' vision and dominant leadership style; it manifests through heroes, myths, symbols, and ceremonies.

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Scott Stephenson: Balancing the Duality of Ethics", draws on press sources [BT, Stephenson; Egan; Heitz]. Through Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme, Wells Fargo managers' pressure on staff to meet new-account quotas, and Mylan's steep EpiPen price rises alongside executive pay increases of over 700 percent, it argues that unethical decisions arise in different parts of a business for different reasons [BT, Egan; Heitz]. Everyone in an organisation is responsible for acting ethically, though primary responsibility rests with the CEO and the chief financial officer [BT]. Verisk Analytics CEO Scott Stephenson describes a “loose–tight” [V] approach: loose in giving employees discretion to make critical decisions in crises where ethics may be involved, tight in building the trust that gives him confidence they will decide responsibly [BT, Stephenson] (Ch 6.4, "Scott Stephenson: Balancing the Duality of Ethics").

### Three managerial roles

Managers' roles fall into three categories (Ch 6.6, "Managerial Roles", Table 6.5):

- *Informational roles*: monitor (gather information), disseminator (provide information internally), spokesperson (transmit information externally).
- *Interpersonal roles*: figurehead (symbolic representation), leader (guide and motivate employees), liaison (go-between among individuals inside and outside the organisation).
- *Decisional roles*: entrepreneur (search for opportunities, initiate change), disturbance handler (handle unexpected events), resource allocator (designate use of resources). Table 6.5 lists these three; the prose adds that in a decisional role a manager may "help resolve conflicts, or negotiate compromises" [V] (Ch 6.6).

Table 6.5 pairs each role with an example [AP] (Ch 6.6, Table 6.5, "The Many Roles Managers Play in an Organization"): monitor, finding out about legal restrictions on new product technology; disseminator, giving current production figures to assembly-line workers; spokesperson, representing the company at a shareholders' meeting; figurehead, cutting the ribbon at a new building’s opening; leader, helping subordinates set monthly performance goals; liaison, representing the retail sales division at a regional sales meeting; entrepreneur, implementing a new production process using new technology; disturbance handler, handling a crisis such as a fire; resource allocator, approving funds to buy computer equipment and hire staff.

### Programmed vs non-programmed decisions

*Programmed decisions* are made in response to routine situations occurring frequently (e.g., hiring procedures); *non-programmed decisions* are required for infrequent, unforeseen, or unusual problems and opportunities and lack precedent (Ch 6.6, "Managerial Decision Making"). Examples of non-programmed: Norfolk Southern's track rescue; Oreck CEO Thomas Oreck's response to Hurricane Katrina (transferred computer systems and call centres to Colorado, planned to move headquarters to Long Beach, deployed UPS distribution from Atlanta).

### Five-step decision-making process

Five steps for both programmed and non-programmed decisions (Ch 6.6, Exhibit 6.7):

1. Recognise or define the problem or opportunity.
2. Gather information to identify alternative solutions or actions.
3. Select one or more alternatives after evaluating strengths and weaknesses.
4. Put the chosen alternative into action.
5. Gather information to obtain feedback on the effectiveness of the chosen plan.

The text warns: "It can be easy (and dangerous) for managers to get stuck at any stage of the decision-making process" [V] — citing analysis paralysis as a particular hazard for entrepreneurs (Ch 6.6).

### Crisis management

Four trends shape contemporary management (Ch 6.8, "Trends in Management and Leadership"): crisis management, outside directors, growing IT use, increasing global management skills.

For crisis management, the text reproduces lessons from named CEOs (Howard Schultz at Starbucks; Gary Loveman at Harrah's; J. W. Marriott; Bob Nardelli at Home Depot; Scott Ford at Alltel; Paul Pressler at Gap; Jim Skinner at McDonald's; et al.) on responding to Hurricane Katrina (Ch 6.8, Table 6.6) [BT]. The table also carries a Hurricane Irma case: Chiles Restaurants COO Robert Baugh talked with staff for several days before the storm to learn who would evacuate, who would stay and who had special needs, used Hot Schedules, a platform all employees log into, to set a timeline for securing the three restaurants and to broadcast reopening, made team leaders responsible for reaching their members, and had food orders cut to minimise loss [BT] (Ch 6.8, Table 6.6). Common threads: invest in notification systems before the next crisis; make life easier for employees; communicate for safety; empower the workforce; be flexible with company assets; prepare for the next big one through postmortems on response efforts.

## Part VII: Organisational structure (Ch 7)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Business Careers profile of Elise Eberwein, executive vice president of people and communications at American Airlines, drawn from company and press sources [BT, Marshall, Fowler and Olson; Eberwein; Slattery; Bradley] (Ch 7, "Elise Eberwein"). It asks what corporate communications has to do with organisational structure and answers "quite a bit at the world’s largest airline" [V]. After the late-2013 merger of American Airlines and US Airways she took over the chief communications job [BT]. A Korn Ferry Institute survey found that nearly 40 percent of senior communications executives at Fortune 500 companies said chief communications officers report directly to the CEO [BT, Marshall, Fowler and Olson]. American’s social media hub of about 30 people reports to Eberwein and may contact any department directly for answers, and senior managers meet weekly to review operations, revenue and people-engagement data [BT] (Ch 7, "Elise Eberwein").

### Five departmentalization types

The organising function decomposes work via division of labor, departmentalization, and delegation (Ch 7.1, "Building Organizational Structures"). Five traditional ways to organize (Ch 7.1, Exhibit 7.5):

1. *Functional*: based on primary functions (marketing, finance, production, sales). Ethan Allen Interiors example.
2. *Product*: based on goods/services produced. ITT's four product divisions.
3. *Process*: based on production process. Gazprom Neft (extraction → refining → marketing); Pixar (technology development → creative development → production).
4. *Customer*: based on primary type of customer served. PNC Financial Services' retail/asset management/corporate banking split.
5. *Geographic*: based on geographic segmentation. Most multinationals.

Many large organisations use combinations. Procter & Gamble's "four pillars": Global Business Units (product), Selling and Market Operations (geographic), Global Business Services (geographic), and Corporate Functions (functional) (Ch 7.1).

The section’s Ethics in Practice feature, "Panera’s Menu Comes Clean", draws on company and press sources [BT, Payne; Jargon; Kell; Furbank]. It holds that a strategic change to a company’s overall philosophy "affects every part of the organizational structure" [V]. In 2015 founder and CEO Ron Shaich announced a "no-no" list of nearly 100 ingredients; two years later Panera declared its menu clean, after reviewing the 450 ingredients in its menu items and reformulating more than 120 of them with its 300 vendors [BT]. The broccoli cheddar soup alone was revised 60 times [BT]. Sara Burnett, director of wellness and food policy, believes Panera can use its voice and purchasing power to improve the wider food system, and the effort also led to a closer look at its supply chain [BT] (Ch 7.1, "Panera’s Menu Comes Clean").

### Line, line-and-staff, matrix, and committee structures

The *line organization* has direct, clear lines of authority and communication flowing from top managers downward (Ch 7.1, "Line-and-Staff Organization"). The *line-and-staff organization* adds staff positions (legal, HR, consulting) that provide advisory and support services to line managers.

The *matrix structure* (project-management approach) combines functional and product departmentalization; each employee has two direct supervisors (functional manager and project manager) (Ch 7.2, "Matrix Structure"). Advantages: teamwork, efficient use of resources, flexibility, ability to balance conflicting objectives, higher performance, opportunities for personal/professional development. Disadvantages: power struggles, confusion among team members, lack of cohesiveness — and the violation of unity-of-command. Unilever moved from matrix to product departmentalization after employees in divisions operating in both North America and Europe were unsure which CEO's decisions took precedence (Ch 7.4) [AE].

A *committee structure* puts authority and responsibility in a group rather than an individual; committees can coordinate complex tasks but may be slow and dominated by individuals (Ch 7.2, "Committee Structure").

### Three types of work teams

The team structure has three evolutionary forms (Ch 7.3, "Types of Teams"):

- *Problem-solving teams*: same department/expertise; same level of hierarchy; meet regularly to share information and recommend improvements; do not make final decisions.
- *Self-managed work teams*: highly autonomous; manage themselves without formal supervision; set goals, plan, schedule, select members, evaluate performance. Approximately 80% of Fortune 1000 companies use some form (Zappos, W. L. Gore).
- *Cross-functional teams*: same hierarchical level but different functional areas; many task forces, organisational committees and project teams. Members often work together only until they solve a problem or complete a project, pooling expertise to develop ideas, solve problems and coordinate complex projects; problem-solving and self-managed teams may also be cross-functional [AP] (Ch 7.3, "Types of Teams").

*Group cohesiveness* is the degree to which members want to stay and resist outside influences (Ch 7.3). When group performance norms are high, cohesiveness has a positive impact on productivity. Cohesiveness is greater when group size is small, individual and group goals are similar, group has high status, rewards are group-based, and the group competes with other groups.

Table 7.1 sets out the strengths and weaknesses of group decision-making, which managers and members must both understand for it to work well [AP] (Ch 7.3, "Understanding Group Behavior", Table 7.1). Strengths: groups bring more information and knowledge; they offer a diversity of perspectives and so generate a greater number of disagreements; group decisions are of higher quality than individual ones; and participation makes acceptance of the decision more likely. Weaknesses: groups take longer to reach a solution; members may pressure others to conform, reducing the likelihood of alternatives; one or a few participants may dominate; and groups lack accountability, since responsibility for outcomes is hard to assign to any one individual [AP] (Ch 7.3, Table 7.1).

The section’s Customer Satisfaction and Quality feature, "Team Approach Flies High at GE Aviation", draws on company and press sources [BT, GE Reports Canada; Kessler; Phillips; Alexander; Jones]. "Teaming" is GE Aviation’s term for self-managed groups of employees who make decisions to work efficiently, maintain quality and meet deadlines; two of its plants have used self-managed teams for more than 30 years, and most of its 77 manufacturing facilities now do [BT]. The goal is "to move decision-making and authority as close to the end-product as possible" [V]. At the Bromont, Quebec, plant, workers have coaches rather than supervisors, teams take on supervisory functions, and team members sit on a joint council that decides matters such as who is promoted or fired [BT]. Hiring for a new plant in Welland, Ontario, tests soft skills as well as technical ones [BT] (Ch 7.3, "Team Approach Flies High at GE Aviation").

### Authority, hierarchy, and span of control

*Authority* is "legitimate power, granted by the organization and acknowledged by employees, that allows an individual to request action and expect compliance" [V] (Ch 7.4, "Authority—Establishing Organizational Relationships"). The *chain of command* extends from one level to the next; *unity of command* means everyone reports to one boss. *Delegation* of authority creates *accountability* — responsibility for outcomes (Ch 7.4).

*Span of control* is the number of employees a manager directly supervises; can range from 2 to 50+. Narrow spans permit higher control but require more management levels (taller structure); wide spans require fewer managers but reduce close supervision (flatter structure) (Ch 7.4, Table 7.2). Five factors determine optimal span: nature of task complexity, location of workers, manager's delegation ability, amount of interaction/feedback required, skill/motivation of workers (Ch 7.5, "Degree of Centralization").

### Centralisation vs decentralisation

*Centralization* concentrates formal authority in one area or level; *decentralization* pushes authority down the hierarchy (Ch 7.5). Benefits of decentralisation can include quicker decision-making, more innovation and creativity, greater flexibility, faster development of lower-level managers, and higher job satisfaction and commitment. "But decentralization can also be risky. If lower-level personnel don’t have the necessary skills and training to perform effectively, they may make costly mistakes" [V] (Ch 7.5). Decentralisation suits large organisations, dynamic environments, managers willing to share power, employees willing to accept responsibility, and geographically dispersed companies.

### Mechanistic vs organic structures

A *mechanistic organization* has high job specialisation, rigid departmentalization, many management levels, narrow spans, centralised decision-making, long chain of command — yields a *tall* structure (Ch 7.6, "Mechanistic versus Organic Structures"). U.S. Army, United Nations are examples. An *organic organization* has low specialisation, loose departmentalization, few levels, wide spans, decentralised decision-making, short chain of command — yields a *flat* structure. Colleges and universities are examples.

Choice depends on strategy (innovation requires organic; cost-control requires mechanistic), size (larger firms tend mechanistic), and external environment (complex/unstable favors organic). W. L. Gore is presented as a counter-example: ~10,000 employees, $3 billion+ revenue, but extremely organic — no bosses, team-based, employees create roles to fill functional gaps (Ch 7.6).

The section’s Managing Change feature, "Google Learns the Alphabet", draws on company and press sources [BT, Clifford; Smith; Hartmans; Rao; Lashinsky; Dunne]. Google’s informal structure fuelled a creative environment, but came under strain as the company grew to more than 60,000 employees in 50 countries [BT]. In 2001 outside CEO Eric Schmidt divided employees into teams by product or function, which worked until acquisitions and new ventures were added [BT]. In 2015 the founders created Alphabet, a holding company that includes Google and other ventures; the move "has provided transparency and an organizational structure that has been simplified" [V], with Sundar Pichai as Google CEO and the founders free to pursue projects such as Project Loon [BT]. The feature judges that the new structure "seems to streamline processes while allowing the various businesses room to grow on their own" [V] (Ch 7.6, "Google Learns the Alphabet").

### Informal organisation

The *informal organization* is "the network of connections and channels of communication based on the informal relationships of individuals inside the organization" [V] (Ch 7.7, "The Informal Organization"). Functions: friendships and social contact, information distribution, status and recognition the formal cannot provide, socialisation of new employees, the *grapevine* (rumor mill). One survey found 47% of employees would believe a grapevine message over a senior leadership speech, with 57% rating their company grapevine as accurate [AP] (Ch 7.7).

### Trends: virtual corporation, virtual teams, outsourcing

*Reengineering* is "the complete redesign of business structures and processes in order to improve operations" [V] (Ch 7.8, "Reengineering Organizational Structure"). The *virtual corporation* is a network of independent companies linked by IT to share skills, costs, and access to one another's markets — Cisco Systems is presented as approaching this form (Ch 7.8).

## Part VIII: Human resource management and labor relations (Ch 8)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Business Careers profile of Andrea Herran, a human resources consultant, drawn from her firm’s site and web profiles [BT, Focus HR; Insureon] (Ch 8, "Andrea Herran, Human Resources Consultant"). A business administration graduate with a psychology minor, she says studying human behaviour helped her "put myself in the position of others" [V]. Over 25 years she rose from administrative assistant in a hotel HR department to director of human resources, then moved into consulting as principal of Focus HR Consulting, advising small firms on HR programmes and legal compliance [BT].
